notes.front: What are Foundry Tools?
notes.back: Cloud-based AI services that help developers build intelligence into applications without needing direct AI or data science skills.
notes.explanation: Developers can add AI capabilities to applications without being AI or data science specialists.
notes.example: Like buying ready-made engine parts instead of designing an engine from scratch.
notes.source: Microsoft, “What are Foundry Tools?”, “What are Foundry Tools?” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-ai-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Foundry Tools are cloud-based artificial intelligence (AI) services that help developers build cognitive intelligence into applications without having direct AI or data science skills or knowledge.

notes.front: What is an AI agent (agent)?
notes.back: Software built on generative AI that can reason over and generate language, use tools to automate tasks, and take suitable action as conditions change.
notes.explanation: Unlike a system that only answers questions, an agent can get things done.
notes.example: Like a personal assistant who not only tells you when your train leaves but books the ticket.
notes.source: Microsoft, “AI agents”, “AI agents” (Microsoft Learn training)
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In an AI agent, what are its instructions?
notes.back: A system prompt that defines the agent’s role and how it should behave.
notes.explanation: They are one of the agent’s three key elements, alongside its model and its tools.
notes.example: Like the brief a temp is handed on their first morning.
notes.source: Microsoft, “AI agents”, “Components of an AI agent” (Microsoft Learn training)
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In an AI agent, what are its tools?
notes.back: What the agent uses to interact with the world, such as knowledge tools and action tools.
notes.explanation: Tools are what let an agent go beyond generating text.
notes.example: Like the phone, the diary and the filing cabinet on an assistant’s desk.
notes.source: Microsoft, “AI agents”, “Components of an AI agent” (Microsoft Learn training)
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is a knowledge tool for an AI agent?
notes.back: A tool that gives the agent access to information, such as a search engine or a database.
notes.explanation: It lets the agent look things up rather than rely only on its model.
notes.example: Like a reference library the assistant can consult.
notes.source: Microsoft, “AI agents”, “Components of an AI agent” (Microsoft Learn training)
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is an action tool for an AI agent?
notes.back: A tool that lets the agent perform tasks, such as sending emails, updating calendars or controlling devices.
notes.explanation: It lets the agent change things in the world, not just find information.
notes.example: Like handing the assistant the keys, not just a map of the building.
notes.source: Microsoft, “AI agents”, “Components of an AI agent” (Microsoft Learn training)
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is a multi-agent system?
notes.back: Several AI agents working together, each with its own speciality, instead of one agent doing everything.
notes.explanation: Together they can handle complex workflows, much like a human team.
notes.example: Like a restaurant kitchen where one cook preps, one grills and one plates.
notes.source: Microsoft, “AI agents”, “Multi-agent systems” (Microsoft Learn training)
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is agentic AI?
notes.back: AI built around agents that act, alone or together, to find information and get work done.
notes.explanation: Microsoft’s training describes it as set to be the next advance in how we use technology.
notes.example: Like moving from a satnav that gives directions to a car that drives you there.
notes.source: Microsoft, “AI agents”, “Multi-agent systems” (Microsoft Learn training)
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is natural language processing (NLP)?
notes.back: Technology for understanding and analysing human language, such as written text.
notes.explanation: Azure Language is the Foundry Tools service that provides it.
notes.example: Like a reader who can skim a letter and tell you who it mentions and how the writer feels.
notes.source: Microsoft, “What is Azure Language in Foundry Tools?”, “What is Azure Language in Foundry Tools?” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-ai-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Azure Language is a cloud-based service that provides Natural Language Processing (NLP) features for understanding and analyzing text. Use this service to help build intelligent applications using the web-based Microsoft Foundry, REST APIs, and client libraries.

notes.front: What is Azure Language in Foundry Tools?
notes.back: A cloud-based service that provides natural language processing features for understanding and analysing text.
notes.explanation: You can use it through the Microsoft Foundry web portal, programming interfaces or client libraries.
notes.example: Like a translator’s desk reference that also highlights names, moods and main points.
notes.source: Microsoft, “What is Azure Language in Foundry Tools?”, “What is Azure Language in Foundry Tools?” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-ai-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Azure Language is a cloud-based service that provides Natural Language Processing (NLP) features for understanding and analyzing text. Use this service to help build intelligent applications using the web-based Microsoft Foundry, REST APIs, and client libraries.

notes.front: What is key phrase extraction?
notes.back: A preconfigured feature that evaluates unstructured text and returns its main concepts as a list.
notes.explanation: The result comes back as a list of concepts.
notes.example: Like the highlighter marks a student leaves on a textbook page.
notes.source: Microsoft, “What is Azure Language in Foundry Tools?”, “Key phrase extraction” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-ai-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Key phrase extraction is a preconfigured feature that evaluates and returns the main concepts in unstructured text, and returns them as a list.

notes.front: What is named entity recognition (NER)?
notes.back: A feature that identifies entities in unstructured text, such as people, places, organisations and quantities, and categorises them.
notes.explanation: Prebuilt NER uses a preset list of entity categories; custom NER can be trained for specialised ones.
notes.example: Like a clerk who reads a letter and files each name under “person”, “company” or “town”.
notes.source: Microsoft, “What is named entity recognition (NER) in Azure Language?”, “What is named entity recognition (NER) in Azure Language?” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-ai-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: The NER feature can identify and categorize entities in unstructured text such as people, places, organizations, and quantities. The prebuilt NER feature has a preset list of recognized entities. The custom NER feature allows you to train the model to recognize specialized entities specific to your use case.

notes.front: What is entity linking?
notes.back: A feature that disambiguates the identity of entities found in text and returns links to Wikipedia.
notes.explanation: It works out which real-world thing a word or phrase refers to.
notes.example: Like a librarian who works out which “Newton” you mean and hands you the right biography.
notes.source: Microsoft, “What is Azure Language in Foundry Tools?”, “Entity linking” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-ai-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Entity linking is a preconfigured feature that disambiguates the identity of entities (words or phrases) found in unstructured text and returns links to Wikipedia.

notes.front: What is personally identifiable information (PII)?
notes.back: Any information that can be used to identify a particular individual, such as a name, address or phone number.
notes.explanation: Email addresses are another example the source gives.
notes.example: Like the details on a passport’s photo page.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Content filtering for Microsoft Foundry Models (classic)”, “Output filters” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-ai-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: PII refers to any information that can be used to identify a particular individual, such as a name, address, phone number, email address

notes.front: What is sentiment analysis in Azure Language?
notes.back: A feature that assigns sentiment labels, such as positive, neutral or negative, to text.
notes.explanation: It picks each label using the highest confidence score.
notes.example: Like a shop manager sorting comment cards into happy, neutral and unhappy piles.
notes.source: Microsoft, “What are sentiment analysis and opinion mining?”, “Sentiment analysis” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-ai-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: The sentiment analysis feature assigns sentiment labels, such as "negative," "neutral," and "positive." The service determines these labels using the highest confidence score. Sentiment is evaluated at both the sentence level and the document level.

notes.front: In sentiment analysis, what is a confidence score?
notes.back: A number between 0 and 1 showing how strongly the service rates a document or sentence as positive, neutral or negative.
notes.explanation: The service returns one for each sentiment, for the document and for each sentence.
notes.example: Like a weather forecast’s “70% chance of rain”.
notes.source: Microsoft, “What are sentiment analysis and opinion mining?”, “Sentiment analysis” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-ai-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: This feature also returns confidence scores between 0 and 1 for each document & sentences within it for positive, neutral, and negative sentiment.

notes.front: What is opinion mining?
notes.back: A feature of sentiment analysis that gives more granular opinions tied to particular words, such as attributes of a product.
notes.explanation: It is also known as aspect-based sentiment analysis.
notes.example: Like a restaurant review read line by line: great food, slow service.
notes.source: Microsoft, “What are sentiment analysis and opinion mining?”, “Opinion mining” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-ai-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Opinion mining is a feature of sentiment analysis, also known as aspect-based sentiment analysis in Natural Language Processing (NLP). This feature provides more granular information about the opinions related to words (such as the attributes of products or services) in text.

notes.front: In Azure Language, what is summarisation?
notes.back: A feature that condenses the information in text and conversations, such as chats and transcripts.
notes.explanation: It works on chats and transcripts as well as on plain text.
notes.example: Like the executive summary at the start of a long report.
notes.source: Microsoft, “What is Azure Language in Foundry Tools?”, “Summarization” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-ai-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Summarization condenses information for text and conversations (chat and transcripts).

notes.front: What is extractive summarisation?
notes.back: Summarising by selecting key sentences from the source and keeping their original positions.
notes.explanation: Every sentence in the summary is an original sentence from the input.
notes.example: Like cutting the three best sentences out of an article and pasting them together.
notes.source: Microsoft, “What is Azure Language in Foundry Tools?”, “Summarization” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-ai-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Extractive summarization creates a summary by selecting key sentences from the document and preserving their original positions.

notes.front: What is abstractive summarisation?
notes.back: Summarising by generating new, concise sentences or phrases that aren’t copied directly from the source.
notes.explanation: The summary is written afresh rather than assembled from the input’s sentences.
notes.example: Like a friend telling you the plot of a film in their own words.
notes.source: Microsoft, “What is Azure Language in Foundry Tools?”, “Summarization” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-ai-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Abstractive summarization generates a summary by producing new, concise, and coherent sentences or phrases that aren't directly copied from the original document.

notes.front: What is conversation summarisation?
notes.back: Summarisation of conversations that recaps long meetings and segments them into timestamped chapters.
notes.explanation: It turns a long meeting into sections marked with times.
notes.example: Like the minutes of a meeting, split into agenda items with times.
notes.source: Microsoft, “What is Azure Language in Foundry Tools?”, “Summarization” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-ai-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Conversation summarization recaps and segments long meetings into timestamped chapters.

notes.front: What is language detection in Azure Language?
notes.back: A prebuilt core capability that identifies the language a text is written in, from more than 100 languages.
notes.explanation: It is one of Azure Language’s prebuilt core capabilities.
notes.example: Like a post-room clerk who glances at a letter and sends it to the right translator.
notes.source: Microsoft, “What is language detection in Azure Language?”, “What is language detection in Azure Language?” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-ai-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Language detection is an Azure Language prebuilt core capability. Language detection can identify more than 100 languages in their primary script.

notes.front: What is text analytics for health?
notes.back: A feature that extracts and labels relevant health information from unstructured text.
notes.explanation: It works on unstructured text, picking out the health details within it.
notes.example: Like a medical secretary who highlights every drug, dose and diagnosis in a doctor’s notes.
notes.source: Microsoft, “What is Azure Language in Foundry Tools?”, “Text analytics for health” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-ai-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Text analytics for health extracts and labels relevant health information from unstructured text.

notes.front: What is question answering in Azure Language?
notes.back: A custom feature that identifies the most suitable answer for user inputs.
notes.explanation: It is typically used to build conversational applications such as chat bots.
notes.example: Like a help-desk worker who finds the best answer in the company’s list of frequently asked questions.
notes.source: Microsoft, “What is Azure Language in Foundry Tools?”, “Question answering” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-ai-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Question answering is a custom feature that identifies the most suitable answer for user inputs. This feature is typically utilized to develop conversational client applications, including social media platforms, chat bots, and speech-enabled desktop applications.

notes.front: What is conversational language understanding (CLU)?
notes.back: A feature for building custom models that predict the overall intention of an utterance and extract important information from it.
notes.explanation: It is customisable: you train it on your own intents and data.
notes.example: Like a receptionist who hears “I need to move Tuesday’s appointment” and knows you want to reschedule, and when.
notes.source: Microsoft, “What is Azure Language in Foundry Tools?”, “Conversational language understanding” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-ai-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Conversational language understanding (CLU) enables users to build custom natural language understanding models to predict the overall intention of an incoming utterance and extract important information from it.

notes.front: The AI-901 outline names six common AI workloads: generative AI, agentic AI, text analysis, speech, computer vision and {{c1::information extraction}}.
notes.explanation: The outline asks you to identify scenarios for each of these workloads.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Study guide for Exam AI-901: Microsoft Azure AI Fundamentals”, “Identify AI workloads” (Microsoft Learn training)
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which Foundry Tool offers speech to text, text to speech, translation and speaker recognition?
notes.back: Speech.
notes.explanation: It is the Foundry Tools service for the speech workload.
notes.source: Microsoft, “What are Foundry Tools?”, “Available Foundry Tools” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-ai-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Speech to text, text to speech, translation, and speaker recognition.

notes.front: Which Foundry Tool analyses content in images and videos?
notes.back: Vision.
notes.explanation: It is the Foundry Tools service for the computer vision workload.
notes.source: Microsoft, “What are Foundry Tools?”, “Available Foundry Tools” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-ai-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Analyze content in images and videos.

notes.front: What are the three key elements of an AI agent?
notes.back: A large language model, instructions and tools.
notes.explanation: The model reasons, the instructions set its role, and the tools let it act on the world.
notes.source: Microsoft, “AI agents”, “Components of an AI agent” (Microsoft Learn training)
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which element of an AI agent acts as its brain, giving it language understanding and reasoning?
notes.back: Its large language model.
notes.explanation: The model uses generative AI; the instructions and tools shape and extend what it does.
notes.source: Microsoft, “AI agents”, “Components of an AI agent” (Microsoft Learn training)
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: How do the agents in a multi-agent system communicate?
notes.back: Through prompts, using generative AI to decide which tasks are needed and which agent does each.
notes.explanation: One agent might gather data, another analyse it and a third act on it.
notes.source: Microsoft, “AI agents”, “Multi-agent systems” (Microsoft Learn training)
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which Azure Language capabilities does Microsoft recommend for new development: core or legacy?
notes.back: Core capabilities.
notes.explanation: Core capabilities are actively evolving and receive ongoing investment and feature updates.
notes.source: Microsoft, “What is Azure Language in Foundry Tools?”, “Core capabilities” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-ai-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Core capabilities are the primary, actively evolving features of Azure Language. These features receive ongoing investment and feature updates, and are recommended for new development and long-term planning.

notes.front: Is named entity recognition a core or a legacy capability of Azure Language?
notes.back: Core.
notes.explanation: Personally identifiable information detection, language detection and text analytics for health are core capabilities too.
notes.source: Microsoft, “What is Azure Language in Foundry Tools?”, “Core capabilities” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-ai-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: PII detection Language detection Named entity recognition (NER) Custom NER Prebuilt NER Text analytics for health

notes.front: Is key phrase extraction a core or a legacy capability of Azure Language?
notes.back: Legacy.
notes.explanation: Sentiment analysis, summarisation, entity linking, question answering and conversational language understanding are legacy too.
notes.source: Microsoft, “What is Azure Language in Foundry Tools?”, “Legacy capabilities” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-ai-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Legacy capabilities are established features that provide a stable, supported base for existing workloads and scenarios. These features are supported for existing implementations and established use cases. Conversational language understanding Custom text classification Entity linking Key phrase extraction Orchestration workflow Question answering Sentiment analysis and opinion mining Summarization

notes.front: When does key phrase extraction retire from Azure Language?
notes.back: 31 March 2029.
notes.explanation: Microsoft advises moving existing workloads, and all new projects, to Microsoft Foundry models.
notes.source: Microsoft, “What is key phrase extraction in Azure Language in Foundry Tools?”, “What is key phrase extraction?” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-ai-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Key phrase extraction retires from Azure Language on March 31, 2029 . To avoid production disruption, migrate existing workloads and direct all new projects to Microsoft Foundry

notes.front: Prebuilt NER recognises entities from a {{c1::preset list}} of categories.
notes.explanation: Custom NER can instead be trained to recognise specialised entities for your use case.
notes.source: Microsoft, “What is named entity recognition (NER) in Azure Language?”, “What is named entity recognition (NER) in Azure Language?” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-ai-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: The NER feature can identify and categorize entities in unstructured text such as people, places, organizations, and quantities. The prebuilt NER feature has a preset list of recognized entities. The custom NER feature allows you to train the model to recognize specialized entities specific to your use case.

notes.front: What three things does PII detection help you do with sensitive data?
notes.back: Identify it, classify it and redact it.
notes.explanation: It works across text, conversations and native documents.
notes.source: Microsoft, “What is PII detection in Azure Language?”, “What is PII detection in Azure Language?” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-ai-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Personally Identifiable Information (PII) detection is an Azure Language core capability that helps you identify, classify, and redact sensitive data across text, conversations, and native documents.

notes.front: Is PII detection a core or a legacy capability of Azure Language?
notes.back: Core.
notes.explanation: It is one of the core capabilities, alongside language detection and named entity recognition.
notes.source: Microsoft, “What is Azure Language in Foundry Tools?”, “Core capabilities” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-ai-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: PII detection Language detection Named entity recognition (NER) Custom NER Prebuilt NER Text analytics for health

notes.front: Which PII feature type returns synchronous results for request-time text such as messages, prompts and logs?
notes.back: Text PII.
notes.explanation: It suits request-time processing of text fields.
notes.source: Microsoft, “What is PII detection in Azure Language?”, “Text PII” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-ai-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Text PII processes string-based payloads and returns synchronous detection and redaction results. Use this feature when your system handles request-time processing for messages, prompts, logs, and other text fields.

notes.front: Which PII feature type handles multi-turn chats and transcripts, where turn boundaries affect detection?
notes.back: Conversation PII.
notes.explanation: It is used for asynchronous workloads that analyse chat and transcript structures.
notes.source: Microsoft, “What is PII detection in Azure Language?”, “Conversation PII” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-ai-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Conversation PII processes multi-turn exchanges and transcript-oriented payloads where turn boundaries and conversation context affect detection and masking behavior. Use this feature for asynchronous workloads that analyze chat and transcript structures.

notes.front: Which PII feature type processes native files and returns redacted output that keeps the document’s structure?
notes.back: Document-based PII.
notes.explanation: It is meant for asynchronous, storage-based pipelines.
notes.source: Microsoft, “What is PII detection in Azure Language?”, “Document-based PII” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-ai-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Document-based PII processes native files and returns redaction output that preserves document structure while also producing machine-readable metadata. Use this feature for asynchronous, storage-based pipelines that handle

notes.front: How does sentiment analysis decide which label to give a sentence or document?
notes.back: It uses the highest confidence score.
notes.explanation: Each of positive, neutral and negative gets a score, and the strongest wins.
notes.source: Microsoft, “What are sentiment analysis and opinion mining?”, “Sentiment analysis” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-ai-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: The sentiment analysis feature assigns sentiment labels, such as "negative," "neutral," and "positive." The service determines these labels using the highest confidence score. Sentiment is evaluated at both the sentence level and the document level.

notes.front: Sentiment is evaluated at both the sentence level and the {{c1::document}} level.
notes.explanation: So one text gets an overall label and a label for each of its sentences.
notes.source: Microsoft, “What are sentiment analysis and opinion mining?”, “Sentiment analysis” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-ai-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: The sentiment analysis feature assigns sentiment labels, such as "negative," "neutral," and "positive." The service determines these labels using the highest confidence score. Sentiment is evaluated at both the sentence level and the document level.

notes.front: Sentiment confidence scores range from {{c1::0 to 1}}.
notes.explanation: There is a score for each of positive, neutral and negative sentiment.
notes.source: Microsoft, “What are sentiment analysis and opinion mining?”, “Sentiment analysis” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-ai-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: This feature also returns confidence scores between 0 and 1 for each document & sentences within it for positive, neutral, and negative sentiment.

notes.front: Opinion mining is also known as {{c1::aspect-based sentiment analysis}}.
notes.explanation: It is a feature of sentiment analysis, not a separate service.
notes.source: Microsoft, “What are sentiment analysis and opinion mining?”, “Opinion mining” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-ai-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Opinion mining is a feature of sentiment analysis, also known as aspect-based sentiment analysis in Natural Language Processing (NLP). This feature provides more granular information about the opinions related to words (such as the attributes of products or services) in text.

notes.front: Which three kinds of input does Azure Language summarisation handle out of the box?
notes.back: Plain text, conversations and native documents.
notes.explanation: Text summarisation, by contrast, only accepts plain text blocks.
notes.source: Microsoft, “What is summarization?”, “What is summarization?” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-ai-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Out of the box, the service provides summarization solutions for three types of genre, plain texts, conversations, and native documents. Text summarization only accepts plain text blocks.

notes.front: In extractive summarisation, what does a sentence’s rank score indicate?
notes.back: How relevant the sentence is to the main topic.
notes.explanation: You can have extracted sentences returned in their original order or by rank.
notes.source: Microsoft, “What is summarization?”, “Key features for text summarization” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-ai-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Rank score: The rank score indicates how relevant a sentence is to the main topic. Text summarization ranks extracted sentences, and you can determine whether they're returned in the order they appear, or according to their rank.

notes.front: Which conversation summarisation feature summarises the issues and resolutions in customer-service conversations?
notes.back: Issue/resolution summarisation.
notes.explanation: It is one of the call-centre-specific features.
notes.source: Microsoft, “What is summarization?”, “Key features for conversation summarization” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-ai-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Call center specific features that give a summary of issues and resolutions in conversations between customer-service agents and your customers.

notes.front: Language detection can identify more than {{c1::100}} languages in their primary script.
notes.explanation: It is a prebuilt core capability of Azure Language.
notes.source: Microsoft, “What is language detection in Azure Language?”, “What is language detection in Azure Language?” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-ai-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Language detection is an Azure Language prebuilt core capability. Language detection can identify more than 100 languages in their primary script.

notes.front: What does language detection return for each document?
notes.back: The main language, with its `ISO 639-1` code, readable name and confidence score, among other details.
notes.explanation: It also returns a script name and script code.
notes.source: Microsoft, “What is language detection in Azure Language?”, “Language detection features” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-ai-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Language detection: For each document, returns the main language, its ISO 639-1 code, readable name, confidence score, script name, and ISO 15924 script code.

notes.front: A word is common to two languages. How can you help language detection pick the right one?
notes.back: Specify a country or region code for where the text comes from.
notes.explanation: Knowing where the text comes from helps the model choose the correct language.
notes.source: Microsoft, “What is language detection in Azure Language?”, “Language detection features” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-ai-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: To help disambiguate language based on the input, you can specify an ISO 3166-1 alpha-2 country/region code. For example, the word "communication" is common to both English and French. Specifying the origin of the text as France can help the language detection model determine the correct language.

notes.front: An app writes a first draft of a cover letter from a few notes about the job. Which AI workload is this?

A) Generative AI
B) Text analysis
C) Information extraction
D) Speech

notes.evidence: Azure Language is a cloud-based service that provides Natural Language Processing (NLP) features for understanding and analyzing text. Use this service to help build intelligent applications using the web-based Microsoft Foundry, REST APIs, and client libraries.

notes.front: A call centre wants recordings of phone calls turned into written text. Which AI workload is this?

notes.front: An agent can look up a customer’s order but can’t cancel it. Which element does it need?
notes.back: An action tool that can cancel orders.
notes.choices:
A) A knowledge tool
B) An action tool
C) Longer instructions
D) A second large language model
notes.choicesExplained: A gives access to information, which it already has. C sets role and behaviour but can’t perform a task. D adds reasoning, not the ability to act.
notes.explanation: Action tools let an agent perform tasks rather than just find information.
notes.source: Microsoft, “AI agents”, “Components of an AI agent” (Microsoft Learn training)
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: An agent searches a company’s product database to answer a question. What kind of tool is it using?
notes.back: A knowledge tool.
notes.explanation: Databases and search engines provide the agent with information.
notes.source: Microsoft, “AI agents”, “Components of an AI agent” (Microsoft Learn training)
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A travel firm uses one agent to gather flight prices, another to compare them and a third to book the best. What is this?
notes.back: A multi-agent system.
notes.choices:
A) A multi-agent system
B) A single agent with three sets of instructions
C) A knowledge tool
D) Opinion mining
notes.choicesExplained: B is one agent, not three collaborating. C is only one kind of tool an agent uses. D analyses opinions in text.
notes.explanation: Several agents, each with its own speciality, collaborate on the workflow.
notes.source: Microsoft, “AI agents”, “Multi-agent systems” (Microsoft Learn training)
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A team is designing a new text-processing architecture that must last for years. Which Azure Language capabilities should it build on?
notes.back: Core capabilities.
notes.explanation: Microsoft recommends core capabilities for new development and long-term planning.
notes.source: Microsoft, “What is Azure Language in Foundry Tools?”, “Core capabilities” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-ai-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Core capabilities are the primary, actively evolving features of Azure Language. These features receive ongoing investment and feature updates, and are recommended for new development and long-term planning.

notes.front: A hotel wants a quick list of the main things guests mention in each review, such as “breakfast” or “parking”. Which feature fits?
notes.back: Key phrase extraction.
notes.choices:
A) Key phrase extraction
B) Language detection
C) Entity linking
D) Text analytics for health
notes.choicesExplained: B only identifies the language. C links entities to Wikipedia. D is for medical text.
notes.explanation: Key phrase extraction returns the main concepts in text as a list.
notes.source: Microsoft, “What is Azure Language in Foundry Tools?”, “Key phrase extraction” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-ai-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Key phrase extraction is a preconfigured feature that evaluates and returns the main concepts in unstructured text, and returns them as a list.

notes.front: An insurer wants names, places and amounts picked out of claim letters and labelled by type. Which feature fits?
notes.back: Named entity recognition.
notes.choices:
A) Sentiment analysis
B) Named entity recognition
C) Summarisation
D) Language detection
notes.choicesExplained: A judges positive or negative tone. C condenses the text. D identifies the language.
notes.explanation: NER identifies entities such as people, places and quantities and categorises them.
notes.source: Microsoft, “What is named entity recognition (NER) in Azure Language?”, “What is named entity recognition (NER) in Azure Language?” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-ai-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: The NER feature can identify and categorize entities in unstructured text such as people, places, organizations, and quantities. The prebuilt NER feature has a preset list of recognized entities. The custom NER feature allows you to train the model to recognize specialized entities specific to your use case.

notes.front: Before sharing support transcripts with an outside analyst, a firm must hide customers’ names and phone numbers. Which feature fits?
notes.back: PII detection, which can redact them.
notes.choices:
A) PII detection
B) Key phrase extraction
C) Entity linking
D) Opinion mining
notes.choicesExplained: B returns main concepts but hides nothing. C links entities to Wikipedia. D analyses opinions.
notes.explanation: PII detection identifies, classifies and redacts sensitive data in text and conversations.
notes.source: Microsoft, “What is PII detection in Azure Language?”, “What is PII detection in Azure Language?” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-ai-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Personally Identifiable Information (PII) detection is an Azure Language core capability that helps you identify, classify, and redact sensitive data across text, conversations, and native documents.

notes.front: A brand wants to know whether each social media post about it is positive, neutral or negative. Which feature fits?
notes.back: Sentiment analysis.
notes.choices:
A) Sentiment analysis
B) Named entity recognition
C) Extractive summarisation
D) Question answering
notes.choicesExplained: B labels entities, not tone. C selects key sentences. D finds answers to questions.
notes.explanation: Sentiment analysis assigns positive, neutral or negative labels.
notes.source: Microsoft, “What are sentiment analysis and opinion mining?”, “Sentiment analysis” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-ai-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: The sentiment analysis feature assigns sentiment labels, such as "negative," "neutral," and "positive." The service determines these labels using the highest confidence score. Sentiment is evaluated at both the sentence level and the document level.

notes.front: A review is mostly glowing but has one furious sentence. What lets you find that sentence?
notes.back: Sentence-level sentiment, returned alongside the document-level label.
notes.explanation: Sentiment is evaluated for each sentence as well as for the whole document.
notes.source: Microsoft, “What are sentiment analysis and opinion mining?”, “Sentiment analysis” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-ai-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: The sentiment analysis feature assigns sentiment labels, such as "negative," "neutral," and "positive." The service determines these labels using the highest confidence score. Sentiment is evaluated at both the sentence level and the document level.

notes.front: A phone maker wants to know that reviewers love the camera but dislike the battery. Which feature gives this detail?
notes.back: Opinion mining.
notes.choices:
A) Opinion mining
B) Language detection
C) Key phrase extraction
D) Conversation summarisation
notes.choicesExplained: B only identifies the language. C lists main concepts without opinions. D condenses conversations.
notes.explanation: Opinion mining ties opinions to specific words, such as product attributes.
notes.source: Microsoft, “What are sentiment analysis and opinion mining?”, “Opinion mining” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-ai-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Opinion mining is a feature of sentiment analysis, also known as aspect-based sentiment analysis in Natural Language Processing (NLP). This feature provides more granular information about the opinions related to words (such as the attributes of products or services) in text.

notes.front: A legal team wants a summary made only of sentences taken word for word from the original report. Which approach fits?
notes.back: Extractive summarisation.
notes.choices:
A) Extractive summarisation
B) Abstractive summarisation
C) Opinion mining
D) Entity linking
notes.choicesExplained: B writes new sentences that aren’t copied. C analyses opinions. D links entities to Wikipedia.
notes.explanation: Extractive summarisation selects key sentences from the source and keeps their positions.
notes.source: Microsoft, “What is Azure Language in Foundry Tools?”, “Summarization” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-ai-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Extractive summarization creates a summary by selecting key sentences from the document and preserving their original positions.

notes.front: A global help desk must send each incoming email to a team that speaks its language. Which feature should run first?
notes.back: Language detection.
notes.choices:
A) Language detection
B) Sentiment analysis
C) Text analytics for health
D) Key phrase extraction
notes.choicesExplained: B judges tone, not language. C is for medical text. D lists main concepts.
notes.explanation: Language detection identifies the language a text is written in.
notes.source: Microsoft, “What is language detection in Azure Language?”, “What is language detection in Azure Language?” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-ai-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Language detection is an Azure Language prebuilt core capability. Language detection can identify more than 100 languages in their primary script.

notes.front: A hospital wants medications and diagnoses labelled in clinical notes, without building its own model. Which feature fits?
notes.back: Text analytics for health.
notes.explanation: It extracts and labels relevant health information from unstructured text.
notes.source: Microsoft, “What is Azure Language in Foundry Tools?”, “Text analytics for health” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-ai-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Text analytics for health extracts and labels relevant health information from unstructured text.

notes.front: A bank’s chat app must tell whether “I lost my card yesterday” means “report a lost card”, and pull out the date. Which feature fits?
notes.back: Conversational language understanding.
notes.explanation: It predicts the overall intention of an utterance and extracts important information from it.
notes.source: Microsoft, “What is Azure Language in Foundry Tools?”, “Conversational language understanding” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-ai-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Conversational language understanding (CLU) enables users to build custom natural language understanding models to predict the overall intention of an incoming utterance and extract important information from it.

notes.front: An article mentions “Mercury”. The app must know whether it means the planet or the element, and link to a reference page. Which feature fits?
notes.back: Entity linking.
notes.explanation: Entity linking disambiguates the identity of entities and returns links to Wikipedia.
notes.source: Microsoft, “What is Azure Language in Foundry Tools?”, “Entity linking” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-ai-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Entity linking is a preconfigured feature that disambiguates the identity of entities (words or phrases) found in unstructured text and returns links to Wikipedia.

notes.front: How does a knowledge tool differ from an action tool?
notes.back: A knowledge tool gives the agent information; an action tool lets it perform tasks.
notes.explanation: One widens what the agent knows, the other what it can do.
notes.source: Microsoft, “AI agents”, “Components of an AI agent” (Microsoft Learn training)
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A text mentions “Amazon”. You need to know whether it means the river or the company, with a link to a reference article. NER or entity linking?
notes.back: Entity linking.
notes.choices:
A) Named entity recognition
B) Entity linking
notes.choicesExplained: A categorises entities into types, such as a place or an organisation, but doesn’t link them to a reference article.
notes.explanation: Entity linking disambiguates which entity is meant and returns a link to Wikipedia.
notes.source: Microsoft, “What is Azure Language in Foundry Tools?”, “Entity linking” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-ai-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Entity linking is a preconfigured feature that disambiguates the identity of entities (words or phrases) found in unstructured text and returns links to Wikipedia.

notes.front: How does extractive summarisation differ from abstractive summarisation?
notes.back: Extractive selects original sentences from the source; abstractive generates new sentences that aren’t copied directly.
notes.explanation: The first assembles the summary; the second writes it.
notes.source: Microsoft, “What is Azure Language in Foundry Tools?”, “Summarization” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-ai-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Extractive summarization creates a summary by selecting key sentences from the document and preserving their original positions. Abstractive summarization generates a summary by producing new, concise, and coherent sentences or phrases that aren't directly copied from the original document.

notes.front: How does opinion mining differ from the rest of sentiment analysis?
notes.back: It is more granular: it ties opinions to specific words, such as attributes of a product, instead of labelling text as a whole.
notes.explanation: Sentiment analysis labels sentences and documents; opinion mining is a finer-grained feature within it.
notes.source: Microsoft, “What are sentiment analysis and opinion mining?”, “Opinion mining” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-ai-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: for positive, neutral, and negative sentiment. Opinion mining Opinion mining is a feature of sentiment analysis, also known as aspect-based sentiment analysis in Natural Language Processing (NLP). This feature provides more granular information about the opinions related to words (such as the attributes of products or services) in text.
